1	# Guitar Hero Bot — System Specification
2	
3	> Top-level overview. For implementation detail of any single subproject, follow the pointers in §3. Each subproject owns its own spec; this document does not duplicate them.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Mission
8	
9	Build an autonomous robot that plays Guitar Hero / Rock Band on a real Wii guitar controller by watching the game video, detecting notes in real time, and pressing physical buttons in sync with the music. The system must run end-to-end without a host PC in the runtime path, produce reference-quality detector output that lighter detectors can be trained against, and provide an on-device operator UI for calibration, mode control, and replay.
10	
11	## 2. Current architecture
12	
13	Three pieces, one runtime brain:
14	
15	```
16	Wii ──HDMI──► ElectronWarp ──HDMI──► TC358743 ──CSI-2──┐
17	                                                       ▼
18	   ┌──────────────────────  marvin (SAM9X75)  ────────────┐
19	   │  HDMI capture → CV detect → timing pipeline → cmds   │
20	   │           ↑              detector-state bus          │
21	   │           │                       ▲                  │
22	   │           │  10.1″ LVDS + maxtouch │                  │
23	   │           │       (operator UI)    │                  │
24	   │           └────────── SD card ─────┘  (recording)    │
25	   └────────┬──────────────────────────┬───────────────────┘
26	            │ T1S bus (cmds)           │ T1S bus (ADC)
27	            │ [FLEXCOM1 UART fallback] │
28	            ▼                          │
29	   ┌──────────────────────────────────┐│
30	   │   fretboard (PIC32CM6408)        │┘
31	   │   ADC scan ↔ open-drain GPIO     │
32	   └────────┬─────────────────────────┘
33	            │ GPIO
34	            ▼
35	   Wii guitar controller ──► Wii (closes the loop)
36	
37	                ◇ off-band: dev PC running fret-tuner
38	                  (calibration / detector tuning / replay)
39	```
40	
41	The diagram is schematic. The shipping link is a **multi-node T1S bus** (§6, [T1S/PoDL
42	link](docs/t1s-podl-link.md)) — marvin the PLCA coordinator, the guitar/fretboard nodes
43	followers — where sensing and actuation are separate node *classes* (see "Node classes"
44	below). A direct FLEXCOM1 UART wire between marvin and the fretboard remains as a build-time
45	fallback transport.
46	
47	**Per-tier role summary:**
48	
49	- **marvin** — SAM9X75 Curiosity host. Owns HDMI capture, the *reference* CV note detector, ingest of detector-node samples, the chord/strum timing pipeline, command emission to the active guitar node, the on-device LVDS+touch operator UI, and reference-data recording to SD. Selects the active detector and the active guitar among whatever is on the bus. The runtime brain.
50	- **fretboard** — PIC32CM6408PL10048 MCU. A **T1S detector node** that also drives: it streams 5-channel phototransistor ADC (note brightness at the strike line) up to marvin, and its on-device model infers the button bitmask and sends it **directly to the `guitar` node over T1S** (peer-to-peer actuation). It has no local Wii-guitar outputs (the standalone open-drain GPIO path was removed when the actuator role moved to the `guitar` node). T1S-only as of 2026-06-17.
51	- **guitar** — PIC32CM PL10 MCU. A **guitar (actuator) node**: receives marvin's button bitmask and drives a Wii guitar controller via open-drain GPIO. New subproject; the actuation half of today's fretboard firmware, on its own node. Multiple guitar variants may coexist on the bus.
52	- **fret-tuner** — Off-band Python tool (FastAPI + browser UI, Linux/macOS PC). Used at the bench for sensor calibration, detector-algorithm tuning, and replay analysis of recordings produced by marvin. Not in the runtime path.
53	
54	**Node classes (T1S bus direction).** marvin is the PLCA coordinator (id 0); followers are typed, and marvin selects the active one of each class:
55	
56	| Class | Role | Node(s) | T1S id / MAC | marvin selection |
57	|---|---|---|---|---|
58	| Detector | observe game state → stream to marvin | `fretboard` (photo-ADC); future variants | 1 / `02:…:01` | active detector (`Detector_SetActive`) |
59	| Guitar (actuator) | receive bitmask → drive a Wii guitar | `guitar` (new); future variants | 2 / `02:…:02` | active guitar (planned) |
60	
61	Detector nodes feed marvin's detector-state bus (each maps to a `detector_id`); guitar nodes are command TX targets. Both classes scale by adding a node-table row. marvin's own `cv_marvin_v1` is a detector too (internal, not a bus node).

121	## 6. Cross-cutting decisions
122	
123	- **Architecture pivot.** The original PC-hosted / Elgato-USB-capture / PS2 / single-PIC-actuator design is retired. Source documents are preserved at [`docs/archive/`](docs/archive/) for design-rationale reference; they are *not* maintained.
124	- **`frame_epoch` is the master sync token.** A 32-bit counter incremented by marvin's video task on every captured ISC frame. Every detector-state record, emitted command, and recording artifact — including data from off-board observers — keys off this token so multi-source data can be aligned post-hoc. Detail in [marvin spec §4.6](firmware/marvin/docs/spec.md).
125	- **Reference data persists on marvin's SD card.** Detector-state + sparse raw BGR888 keyframes (default 1 keyframe/sec) + raw ADC stream + emitted commands. Off-board detectors record their own data keyed by `frame_epoch` and align offline.
126	- **Centralized timing on marvin, with a fretboard-takeover fallback.** marvin runs the chord-window FIFO and strum scheduler by default; an operator-mode toggle hands timing back to fretboard's standalone `fret_button.c` while marvin still records observations.
127	- **Operating modes are independent toggles**, not a global state machine: `detect_enable`, `marvin_timing_enable`, `actuate_enable`, `record_enable`. Named modes (idle / calibrate / dry-run / play / replay / record) are presets over them.
128	- **Sensing and actuation are separate node classes on the T1S bus.** Detector nodes (e.g. `fretboard`) stream observations; guitar nodes (e.g. `guitar`) actuate. A detector may also *command* a guitar directly (peer-to-peer): the `fretboard`'s on-device model infers the bitmask and sends it to the `guitar` node, while marvin can also command the guitar (its timing pipeline). **The split is live and both ends are on T1S** (2026-06-17): marvin (PLCA coordinator) sends its command to the `guitar` node, and the `fretboard` (T1S-only) streams data to marvin + drives the guitar directly. **Open:** no active-source arbitration yet — both marvin and the fretboard can address the guitar, so only one drives at a time (marvin-side active-detector/active-guitar selection is the follow-up; the fretboard's SW0 is an interim manual arm). Addressing/node-table detail in [`docs/t1s-podl-link.md`](docs/t1s-podl-link.md) §7.1.
129	- **The marvin↔node link runs on 10BASE-T1S (built; PoDL planned).** A LAN8651B1 MAC-PHY at each end over SPI + the OPEN Alliance TC6 driver + a minimal L2 header (no IP stack); the existing 1-byte/17-byte frame formats ride inside the Ethernet payload unchanged. **Working today between marvin and the `guitar` node** (command + presence heartbeat + diagnostics); the fretboard detector follows. Motivation, in order: PoDL would carry power *and* data on one pair; better noise/cable tolerance; PLCA multidrop headroom; demonstrating 10BASE-T1S + PoDL inside a larger Microchip system. Bandwidth is not a driver (UART had ~12× headroom). **PoDL** (dumb, fixed-voltage, no SCCP) is design-direction only — not built; the link is separately powered for now. Detail in [`docs/t1s-podl-link.md`](docs/t1s-podl-link.md).
130

152	
153	## 8. What this is *not*
154	
155	To anchor against the original architecture (preserved in `docs/archive/`):
156	
157	- **Not PC-hosted.** marvin is the runtime brain; no host PC is required for play.
158	- **Not USB-capture / Elgato.** Video is captured directly off HDMI via a TC358743 → MIPI CSI-2 path into the SAM9X75's ISC.
159	- **Not PS2.** The supported console is the Nintendo Wii (with an ElectronWarp component → HDMI converter).
160	- **Not a single-MCU sense+actuate node.** Sensing and timing live on marvin; sensing (detector nodes) and actuation (guitar nodes) are separating onto distinct nodes on the T1S bus, not one solo controller (with the explicit exception of fretboard's standalone-fallback mode during the transition).
161	- **Not OpenCV / Python at runtime.** CV runs natively on the SAM9X75 (Cortex-A5). Python (`fret-tuner`) is a bench tool only.

1	# fauxmote — Specification
2	
3	> What fauxmote *is* (purpose, hardware, interfaces, success criteria, milestones).
4	> The running diary of decisions and progress lives in [`docs/journal.md`](docs/journal.md) — read it alongside this on any non-trivial task.
5	
6	## 1. Purpose
7	
8	fauxmote is an **ESP32 firmware that emulates a Nintendo Wiimote with an attached
9	Guitar Hero guitar extension**, speaking Bluetooth straight to a real Wii console.
10	It is a **parallel proof-of-concept** alternative to the existing actuation path:
11	today the [fretboard](../fretboard/SPEC.md) MCU physically presses buttons on a
12	*real* Wii guitar controller via open-drain GPIO. fauxmote instead *becomes* the
13	controller — eventually driven by [marvin](../marvin/docs/spec.md)'s high-level
14	fret/strum commands, removing the physical actuator + real controller from the loop.
15	
16	The fretboard GPIO-press path stays authoritative until fauxmote is proven; nothing
17	in marvin/fretboard/edge-ai changes as part of this subproject.
18	
19	## 2. Hardware
20	
21	| Component | Detail |
22	|---|---|
23	| Board | **Adafruit ESP32 Feather V2** (product 5400) — *original* dual-core ESP32 (Tensilica LX6), 8 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM, USB-C. |
24	| Radio | ESP32 has a **Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR)** radio — required, because the Wiimote link is Classic HID. (ESP32-S3/C3 are BLE-only and would *not* work.) |
25	| Wii console | Real retail Wii; pairing via the sync button or the controller's 1+2 button. |
26	
27	## 3. The link fauxmote emulates (verified protocol facts)
28	
29	- **Transport:** Bluetooth Classic **HID** over L2CAP — PSM `0x11` (control),
30	  PSM `0x13` (data). Input reports (device→host) prefixed `0xa1`; output reports
31	  (host→device) prefixed `0xa2`.
32	- **Identity the Wii expects (SDP):** device name `Nintendo RVL-CNT-01`,
33	  VID `0x057e`, PID `0x0306`, matching Class-of-Device, and the Wiimote HID report
34	  descriptor.
35	- **Pairing PIN (legacy):** the PIN is a BD_ADDR in **reverse byte order** (raw 6
36	  bytes). The 1+2 temporary-pair flow uses the *Wiimote's own* address — which
37	  fauxmote knows — so fauxmote can answer the GAP PIN request itself.
38	- **Guitar extension:** identity bytes `00 00 A4 20 01 03` at register offset `0xfa`
39	  of the `0xa4` extension space. The 6-byte report (frets G/R/Y/B/O, strum up/down,
40	  whammy in byte 3, touch bar, analog stick, +/− buttons; **byte 0/1 bits 7-6 = 1**
41	  to identify a GH3 Les Paul) rides inside any extension-bearing data report — GH3
42	  streams mode `0x37`.
43	- **Guitar extension encryption (required for GH3):** GH3 writes `0x55`→`0xf0` and
44	  reads the ID in the clear (to tell GH3 vs GHWT), then `0xAA`→`0xf0` plus a 16-byte
45	  key to `0x40`-`0x4f`. After that the streamed report bytes *and* the `0x20`
46	  calibration must be encrypted with the standard Wii extension cipher; plaintext
47	  reads as garbage in-game.
48	
49	References: wiibrew [`Wiimote`](https://wiibrew.org/wiki/Wiimote) and
50	[`Guitar Hero (Wii) Guitars`](https://wiibrew.org/wiki/Wiimote/Extension_Controllers/Guitar_Hero_(Wii)_Guitars).
51	
52	## 4. Interfaces
53	
54	- **Downstream (fauxmote → Wii):** Bluetooth Classic HID, as above.
55	- **Upstream (commands → fauxmote):** the **marvin command link** — a layered
56	  message protocol, **UART first** (T1S later), specified in
57	  [`docs/marvin-fauxmote-link.md`](../../docs/marvin-fauxmote-link.md). marvin sends a
58	  tiny fixed `GUITAR` hot message (fret/strum mask + whammy + aux), a `WIIMOTE` nav
59	  message (core buttons/D-pad/stick), and `LINK_CMD` (Bluetooth link management:
60	  pair/stop/reconnect/unlink/ext); fauxmote returns `STATUS`. Absolute/latest-wins;
61	  a link timeout releases all inputs. The link is a second front-end over the same
62	  module APIs the CLI uses. Early bring-up still uses the local CLI (§ below).
63	- **Debug:** USB-C CDC serial for flashing + logs (`idf.py monitor`).
64	
65	## 5. Software
66	
67	- **Framework:** ESP-IDF (v6.x; developed against v6.0.1), Bluedroid stack in **Bluetooth-Classic-only** mode
68	  (BLE disabled).
69	- **BT architecture (settled in Phase 1):** `esp_hidd` is *not* usable — the Wii
70	  rejects its SDP record and its hardcoded HID attributes/descriptor limits don't
71	  fit a Wiimote. Instead fauxmote serves a **byte-exact Wiimote SDP record** built
72	  via Bluedroid's internal `SDP_*` database API (`wiimote_sdp.c`; needs
73	  `CONFIG_BT_SDP_PAD_LEN`/`ATTR_LEN` raised) and handles HID over **raw L2CAP**
74	  (`esp_bt_l2cap`) on PSM 0x11 (control) / 0x13 (interrupt). Legacy PIN pairing
75	  (SSP off; PIN = host BD_ADDR reversed). Detail + the record bytes in
76	  [`docs/wiimote-sdp.md`](docs/wiimote-sdp.md) and the journal.
77	- **Extension architecture:** extensions register with the base Wiimote through a
78	  small interface (`wiimote_ext.h`: register bank + report/button/reset hooks); the
79	  guitar lives in `guitar.c`, leaving `wiimote.c` extension-agnostic. The Wii
80	  extension cipher (`ext_crypto.c`) lives in the base — it captures the host's key
81	  handshake and encrypts outgoing extension data (streamed bytes + register reads),
82	  which Guitar Hero 3 requires.
83	- **marvin command link:** `main/marvin_link.c` is a FreeRTOS task that owns UART1,
84	  the framing/CRC, and message parse/dispatch, driving the same module APIs the CLI
85	  uses and emitting `STATUS`. Started at boot via `MarvinLink_Start()` (`main.c`).
86	  Protocol in [`docs/marvin-fauxmote-link.md`](../../docs/marvin-fauxmote-link.md).
87	- **Allocation:** application code follows the project's **static-allocation**

Here's a functional summary suitable for export compliance documentation, covering the whole system including fauxmote.

---

## Functional Summary — Guitar Hero Bot

**What it is:** A hobby/educational robot that plays the video game Guitar Hero (or Rock Band) on a Nintendo Wii by itself — no human and no PC needed while it's playing. It watches the game on screen, figures out which notes are coming, and "presses the buttons" in time with the music.

- **Watches the game video.** A small adapter takes the Wii's HDMI video output and feeds it into the main controller board (a Microchip SAM9X75, called "marvin"). This is a standard video capture path — the same kind of video signal a TV would receive.

- **Recognizes the notes.** marvin runs computer-vision software that looks at the incoming video and detects the colored note markers as they reach the "strike line," then works out the timing of each strum and chord.

- **Sends button-press commands.** marvin sends simple on/off button commands ("press green," "strum now") to a separate small microcontroller node over a two-wire industrial Ethernet link (10BASE-T1S). No internet, no wireless — just a short wire between boards inside the demo.

- **Presses the physical buttons.** The actuator node ("guitar") drives simple electrical switches that press the buttons on a real Wii guitar controller, exactly as a human's fingers would. The Wii sees an ordinary controller.

- **Has an operator screen.** marvin drives a 10.1" touchscreen used by the operator to calibrate, pick modes, and watch what the robot is doing. Purely a local user interface.

- **Records reference data.** For development, marvin can save what it saw and what it did to an SD card, so the behavior can be reviewed later on a bench PC.

- **Bench-only tools.** A Python tool ("fret-tuner") and log viewers run on a normal laptop for calibration and tuning. These are development aids and are not part of the robot while it plays.

- **Alternate "virtual controller" experiment (fauxmote).** A separate proof-of-concept uses an off-the-shelf ESP32 Wi-Fi/Bluetooth board to *pretend to be* a Wii controller over Bluetooth, instead of physically pressing buttons. This is an optional, parallel experiment, not the main demo path.

**Overall:** commodity building blocks — a video capture chip, general-purpose microcontrollers, computer-vision software, simple electrical switches, and a wired board-to-board link — assembled to autonomously play a music video game.

---

## Encryption statement

**The core system (the button-pressing robot) uses no encryption.** All of its interfaces — HDMI video capture, the internal 10BASE-T1S wired link between boards, the USB debug/log connection, and SD-card storage — carry data in the clear. There is no cryptographic functionality in the main runtime path.

**The optional fauxmote proof-of-concept does involve encryption, in two standard/incidental ways:**
- **Bluetooth Classic link security** — provided by the off-the-shelf ESP32 Bluetooth stack (ESP-IDF/Bluedroid). This is the standard, framework-supplied pairing/link encryption inherent to any Bluetooth device; it is not custom-developed here.
- **Wii controller "extension cipher"** — a simple, proprietary obfuscation scheme (documented publicly by the homebrew community) that the game console requires for controller add-on data. It is a lightweight controller-data scramble, not general-purpose data-security encryption, and is used solely to make the emulated controller acceptable to the game.

## Functional Summary — Guitar Hero Bot

**What it is:** A hobby/educational robot that plays the video game Guitar Hero (or Rock Band) on a Nintendo Wii by itself — no human and no PC needed while it's playing. It watches the game on screen, figures out which notes are coming, and acts as the game controller in time with the music.

- **Watches the game video.** A small adapter takes the Wii's HDMI video output and feeds it into the main controller board (a Microchip SAM9X75, called "marvin"). This is a standard video capture path — the same kind of video signal a TV would receive.

- **Recognizes the notes.** marvin runs computer-vision software that looks at the incoming video and detects the colored note markers as they reach the "strike line," then works out the timing of each strum and chord.

- **Decides the button presses.** marvin turns what it sees into simple controller commands ("hold green," "strum now"), with the correct timing.

- **Sends commands to the controller emulator.** marvin sends those commands over a short wired link to a small off-the-shelf Wi-Fi/Bluetooth board (an ESP32, running the "fauxmote" firmware). No internet is involved — just a wire between the two boards inside the demo.

- **Acts as the Wii controller (over Bluetooth).** fauxmote pretends to be a genuine Nintendo Wii Remote with a Guitar Hero guitar attachment, and connects to the Wii over Bluetooth. The Wii sees an ordinary wireless controller and responds to the button presses the robot decided. This replaces any physical button-pressing hardware.

- **Has an operator screen.** marvin drives a 10.1" touchscreen used by the operator to calibrate, pick modes, and watch what the robot is doing. Purely a local user interface.

- **Records reference data.** For development, marvin can save what it saw and what it did to an SD card, so the behavior can be reviewed later on a bench PC.

- **Bench-only tools.** A Python tool ("fret-tuner") and log viewers run on a normal laptop for calibration and tuning. These are development aids and are not part of the robot while it plays.

**Overall:** commodity building blocks — a video capture chip, a general-purpose microcontroller, computer-vision software, and an off-the-shelf Bluetooth board emulating a game controller — assembled to autonomously play a music video game on a real Wii.

---

## Encryption statement

**The demo does use encryption**, entirely on the Bluetooth link between the controller-emulator board and the Wii. It is standard/incidental, not custom-developed cryptography:

- **Bluetooth Classic link security** — provided by the off-the-shelf ESP32 Bluetooth stack (ESP-IDF/Bluedroid). This is the standard pairing/link encryption inherent to any Bluetooth device; it is not implemented by this project.

- **Wii controller "extension cipher"** — a simple, proprietary obfuscation scheme (publicly documented by the homebrew community) that the Wii game requires for controller add-on data. It is a lightweight controller-data scramble used solely to make the emulated controller acceptable to the game, not a general-purpose data-security feature.

**The rest of the system uses no encryption.** The HDMI video capture, the wired link between marvin and the emulator board, the USB debug/log connection, and SD-card storage all carry data in the clear.

1	# Export Compliance — Functional Summary
2	
3	> Plain-language description of the Guitar Hero Bot demo for export compliance
4	> documentation, including an explicit statement of encryption usage.
5	
6	## Functional Summary — Guitar Hero Bot
7	
8	**What it is:** A hobby/educational robot that plays the video game Guitar Hero 
9	on a Nintendo Wii by itself — no human and no PC needed while it's playing.
10	It watches the game on screen, figures out which notes are coming, and acts as the game
11	controller in time with the music. A human can play against the robot using
12	a standard Guitar Hero guitar controller. The Nintendo Wii console and the human's guitar
13	controller are standard, unmodified, off-the-shelf consumer Wii components.
14	
15	- **Watches the game video.** A small adapter takes the Wii's HDMI video output and
16	  feeds it into the main controller board (Microchip SAM9X75). This
17	  is a standard video capture path — the same kind of video signal a TV would receive.
18	
19	- **Recognizes the notes.** marvin runs computer-vision software that looks at the
20	  incoming video and detects the colored note markers as they reach the "strike line,"
21	  then works out the timing of each strum and chord.
22	
23	- **Decides the button presses.** marvin turns what it sees into simple controller
24	  commands ("hold green," "strum now"), with the correct timing.
25	
26	- **Sends commands to the controller emulator.** marvin sends those commands over a
27	  short two-wire module bus (10BASE-T1S single-pair Ethernet, a standard wired
28	  networking link) to a small off-the-shelf ESP32 board that acts as the controller
29	  emulator.
30	
31	- **Modular, expandable bus.** The two-wire bus is modular: additional boards can plug
32	  into the same wired link. Planned add-on modules include beat detection (sensing the
33	  song's rhythm), puppet animation (driving mechanical show figures), and a light-show
34	  controller (driving decorative/stage lighting) — all to make the demo a more engaging
35	  interactive show. These are local, wired modules; none add internet connectivity or
36	  encryption.
37	
38	- **Has an operator screen.** marvin drives a 10.1" touchscreen used by the operator to
39	  calibrate, pick modes, and watch what the robot is doing. Purely a local user
40	  interface.
41	
42	**Overall:** commodity building blocks — a video capture chip, a general-purpose
43	microcontroller, computer-vision software, and an off-the-shelf Bluetooth board
44	emulating a standard Guitar Hero guitar controller — assembled to autonomously play a
45	music video game on a standard, unmodified Nintendo Wii, optionally against a human
46	competitor using a standard guitar controller.
47	
48	## System block diagram
49	
50	```mermaid
51	flowchart TD
52	    Wii["Nintendo Wii console<br/>(standard, unmodified)"]
53	    Human["Human competitor<br/>standard guitar controller"]
54	
55	    subgraph Robot["Guitar Hero Bot"]
56	      HDMI["HDMI &rarr; CSI-2<br/>capture adapter"]
57	      marvin["marvin &mdash; SAM9X75 host<br/>HDMI capture &middot; CV note detection &middot; timing"]
58	      UI["10.1&quot; touchscreen<br/>operator UI"]
59	      T1S{{"Modular T1S bus<br/>10BASE-T1S single-pair Ethernet"}}
60	      ESP["ESP32 &mdash; controller emulator<br/>(fauxmote)"]
61	      Beat["Beat detection<br/>(planned)"]
62	      Puppet["Puppet animation<br/>(planned)"]
63	      Light["Light-show controller<br/>(planned)"]
64	    end
65	
66	    Wii -->|HDMI video| HDMI
67	    HDMI -->|CSI-2| marvin
68	    marvin --- UI
69	    marvin --- T1S
70	    T1S --- ESP
71	    T1S -.-> Beat
72	    T1S -.-> Puppet
73	    T1S -.-> Light
74	    ESP ==>|Bluetooth &middot; encrypted| Wii
75	    Human ==>|Bluetooth &middot; encrypted| Wii
76	```
77	
78	Solid lines are built today; dashed lines are planned add-on modules on the same bus.
79	The only encrypted links (thick arrows) are the Bluetooth connections to the Wii.
80	
81	## Encryption statement
82	
83	**The demo does use encryption**, entirely on the Bluetooth link between the
84	controller-emulator board and the Wii. It is standard/incidental, not custom-developed
85	cryptography:
86	
87	- **Bluetooth Classic link security** — provided by the off-the-shelf ESP32 Bluetooth
88	  stack (ESP-IDF/Bluedroid). This is the standard pairing/link encryption inherent to
89	  any Bluetooth device; it is not implemented by this project.
90	
91	- **Wii controller "extension cipher"** — a simple, proprietary obfuscation scheme
92	  (publicly documented by the homebrew community) that the Wii game requires for
93	  controller add-on data. It is a lightweight controller-data scramble used solely to
94	  make the emulated controller acceptable to the game, not a general-purpose
95	  data-security feature.
96	
97	**The rest of the system uses no encryption.** The HDMI video capture, the wired link
98	between marvin and the emulator board, and the USB debug/log connection all carry data
99	in the clear.
100
```
</details></tool-use>
